candidates.title: Driver Pulls Up Directly to Firehouse When His Tesla Inexplicably Bursts Into Flames
candidates.raw_excerpt: At this point, it’s a pretty well known fact that electric vehicles — and, at least in the popular imagination, Teslas especially — have a nagging habit of erupting into flames. One Tesla owner in Maine evidently has that concern hovering in the back of their mind every time they leave the driveway. While driving around the town of Tremont in a sleek red Model S, an unnamed driver hit an object on the road which punctured the vehicle’s lithium-ion battery, local station WABI5 reported . As most EV drivers are hopefully aware, any kind of damage to a car’s battery can easily spark a fire fueled by thermal runaway , resulting in a uniquely dangerous inferno that can be difficult to put out. Luckily, this driver kept their head, driving straight to the Tremont fire station where the high-voltage battery immediately burst into flames, Bangor Daily News reported . With help from the nearby Southwest Harbor Fire Department, the crew of the Tremont Volunteer Fire Department sprang into action, shutting down the road and dousing the Tesla using an arsenal of firehoses. Based on photos of the incident, it seems the Tesla was totaled, but the driver is said to be doing alright. The Tremont fire comes just days after an exploding Tesla in Seattle sent two firefighters to the hospital. That particular EV was parked inside an attached garage at the time, resulting in a two-alarm housefire that displaced an unfortunate family. All told, if you drive an EV, it’s probably smart to have the address of the nearest fire department drilled into your head — especially if it’s a Tesla. candidates.raw_excerpt: Optus , an Australian based telco and satellite player, has achieved a key milestone in the area of satellite life extension. It has completed the first phase of Project Aurora, with the successful undocking of the Mission Extension Vehicle (MEV) from the Optus D3 satellite. Phase two is now underway, Optus is on track to extend the life of Optus D3 by up to six years through the installation of a Mission Extension Pod (MEP) in late 2027. Optus revealed the latest details of Project Aurora, Aug. 12. Once installed, the MEP will augment the propulsion capabilities of the D3 satellite, effectively acting as an additional fuel source and extending the satellite’s operational life by up to six years, helping to secure service continuity into the 2030s. Optus is working with Northrop Grumman on this initiative. The Northrop Grumman operated MRV is designed to service multiple satellites in orbit using sophisticated robotics, installing MEPs that provide propulsion support and extend mission lifespans. After docking, the Optus-owned and controlled MEP will play a critical role in maintaining the long-term performance of the D3 satellite. “The successful undocking of the MEV from Optus D3 marks the completion of the first phase of Project Aurora and is a significant achievement in our mission to increase the resilience of our sovereign satellite fleet. Combined with the recent successful launch of the MRV and Optus’ Mission Extension Pod, we are continuing to break new ground in satellite life extension in partnership with Northrop Grumman. These milestones demonstrate how innovative technologies can maximize the value of existing satellite assets while supporting long-term service continuity for customers,” Harvey Wright, Executive General Manager, Satellite, Optus, said in a statement. candidates.raw_excerpt: Comet 220P/McNaught soaring over Namibia on August 8, 2026. (Image credit: Gerald Rhemann and Michael Jäger) What a view. Astrophotographers in Namibia have captured a bright green comet soaring overhead in a spectacular new photograph. What is it? In this incredible new photograph is the comet 220P/McNaught. Discovered by Australian astronomer Robert H. McNaught, the comet orbits our sun once every 5.5 years. Back in June, the comet reached perihelion, or the closest point in its orbit around the sun. Around that time, the comet experienced a large outburst, which brightened it about 8,000 times. The comet brightened back up this August to about 600 times its normal brightness — and it was during this period when astrophotographers Gerald Rhemann and Michael Jäger captured it streaking across the night sky over Namibia. To capture the moment, the pair used a 12-inch Astrograph telescope with a ZWO ASI 6200 MM Pro camera. Why is it incredible? It's not every day you see a comet in the night sky . Even if one is overhead, often they're too tricky or too far away to spot without a telescope, and even then it can be a challenge. It's also incredible that the moment captured in the new image showcases the comet 220P/McNaught with such spectacular clarity and detail. It must have been something truly special to witness. While spotting a comet like this might not happen every day, we can sometimes see the debris trailing behind a comet as its tail burns up in our atmosphere. These burnt comet bits are actually the "shooting stars" we see in the night sky during a meteor shower. Right now, the Perseids meteor shower is on its annual parade across the night sky. candidates.raw_excerpt: The Perseid meteor shower, one of the most prolific and impressive meteor showers of the year, peaks tonight! Widely regarded as one of the best meteor showers of the year, the Perseids can produce up to 100 meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions and weather permitting. This year's display is particularly favorable because the shower peaks on the night of the new moon, leaving skies free from bright moonlight that can wash out fainter meteors . What time should I look? The Perseids can produce meteors throughout the night, but the best viewing begins around 11 p.m. local time, with activity increasing after midnight and continuing until the predawn hours. Under dark, clear skies, patient observers could see dozens of meteors every hour with the highest rates expected just before dawn. Where do they come from? The annual show occurs as Earth passes through a trail of comet dust and rocky debris left behind by Comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle. Every year, our planet plows through this stream of cometary material, causing tiny fragments — many no larger than a grain of sand — to slam into Earth's atmosphere at around 133,000 mph (214,000 km/h). As these particles compress and heat the air in front of them, they burn up high above Earth's surface, creating the brilliant streaks of light we know as meteors or shooting stars. Every year, Earth passes through the path of Comet Swift-Tuttle. With the Perseid meteor shower's peak occurring when Earth passes through the densest, dustiest area. The latest 2D cosmic map represents the culmination of 13 years of observations and data processing. Installed on the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona, DESI measures the spectra of galaxies and quasars . By determining their redshifts — how much their light has been stretched as the universe expands — astronomers can calculate their distances and transform a flat view of the sky into a 3D map of the cosmos. Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI; Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI) With a glorious mane of glowing purple gas and dust, the Lion Nebula sparkles on the cosmic savanna in this new image captured by the James Webb Space Telescope . What is it? This new image highlights the stunning beauty of the Lion Nebula (formally named NGC 2392), which earned its nickname thanks to its vaguely lion-head-shaped "face" and surrounding, fuzzy "mane". At the center of this lion's face lies its nose, a bright purple spot. This spot is actually the remnant of a dying star that's radiating energy outward and powering the cosmic structure. This oxygen-rich remnant is a white dwarf, or the hot core of a dying star. As a star like this dies, it becomes unstable and sheds its outer layers, blasting gas and dust outward to create a planetary nebula. The white dwarf got left behind after the nose in the center of the "lion's" face expelled energy and created a big bubble of ionized gas around itself. Over time, the lion's face will continue to expand. Astronomers estimate that in about 10,000 years, the lion might dissipate entirely. Why is it incredible? This isn't the first time we've seen the Lion Nebula. Back in 2000, for instance, the Hubble Space Telescope took a close look at the nebula. However, the JWST snapped this image of the nebula using two of its state-of-the-art instruments: the NIRCam (Near Infrared Camera) and MIRI (Mid Infrared Instrument). And the new view gives us a very detailed look at the nebula. With these new instruments, we can see details we never saw in the Hubble's view of the Lion Nebula — like certain dust and gas features.

candidates.title: Chinese LM-7A Rocket Fails
candidates.raw_excerpt: China experienced a launch failure today of their relatively new Long March 7A rocket. Introduced in 2020, the first launch failed, but the track record since then has been perfect. The cause is under investigation. Videos of the launch posted on X show the vehicle exploding soon after launch from the Wenchang Satellite Launch Center on Hainan Island. Jonathan McDowell of Jonathan’s Space Report told SpacePolicyOnline.com there appeared to be a structural failure when the rocket reached maximum dynamic pressure or MaxQ. The cause is under investigation, but could have implications for future launches especially if it’s a design issue. The LM-7 is used primarily to send Tianzhou cargo missions to China’s Tiangong space station and the 7A version launches satellites, including military satellites, to geostationary transfer orbit. Since the original failure in 2020, it’s had more than a dozen successes. Today’s launch was of ChinaSat-4B. The South China Morning Post said the explosion happened just 90 seconds after liftoff at 8:00 pm Beijing Time and images “apparently taken from long-wave infrared tracking footage of the launch appeared to show the rocket snapping near its upper section moments before it was destroyed.” SCMP added that the satellite was to provide communications services, and satellites in the series with low numbers are thought to be for military purposes. Whether the failure will have any impact on China’s plans to launch the Chang’e-7 robotic mission to the Moon’s South Pole later this month is unclear. Chang’e-7 will launch on a different rocket, Long March 5, but the LM-5 Solid Rocket Boosters use the same engines as LM-7A.

candidates.raw_excerpt: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is a NASA infrared space telescope with a 2.4 m (7.9 ft) wide field of view primary mirror and two scientific instruments. The Coronagraphic Instrument (CGI) is a high-contrast, small field of view camera and spectrometer covering visible and near-infrared wavelengths using novel starlight-suppression technology. Roman objectives include a search for extra-solar planets using gravitational microlensing, and probing the expansion history of the Universe and the growth of cosmic structure, with the goal of measuring the effects of dark energy, the consistency of general relativity, and the curvature of spacetime.

candidates.title: Scientists Warn That New Satellites Could Cause Eye Damage for People on the Ground
candidates.raw_excerpt: Last month, the Federal Communications Commission approved an experimental and controversial new satellite being developed by venture Reflect Orbital to reflect sunlight down onto the Earth to illuminate patches of it at night for paying customers. The purported goal is to allow solar farms to continue generating electricity even after nightfall and provide illumination during emergencies. Those may sound like noble ideas on the surface, but the concept comes with major downsides as well. One is that such bright satellites could easily wreck deep space observations. Astronomers were appalled at the news , with the FCC receiving nearly nearly 2,000 public comments criticizing the proposal, as Wired reported at the time. And it’s not just professional astronomers that could be affected, as experts told The Verge . Amateur astronomers gazing up at the prototype mirror satellite, dubbed Eärendil-1 — continuing Silicon Valley’s obsession with borrowing names from JRR Tolkien’s “Lord of the Rings” — could easily be blinded. Even looking through a 12-inch telescope, a common type used by enthusiasts, could result in permanent eye damage. It’s a considerable risk to human health that makes the FCC’s approval “extraordinary,” as Royal Astronomical Society deputy executive director Robert Massey told The Verge . It’s a risk experts have known for decades now. Case in point, observing a similar proposed Russian prototype , dubbed Znamya, could cause damage equivalent to staring at the Sun around a total eclipse, according to a 2000 research article by the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada. (Russia launched two experimental Znamya space mirror satellites in the 1990s, but later abandoned the program.) "We can't explicitly say that we are seeing a decrease in star formation because of M32.
